extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in humor theory (psychology, linguistics, philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedia overview summarizing multiple theoretical accounts of what humor is, when laughter occurs, and mechanisms that make things funny (psychological, linguistic, evolutionary, social). Useful as a reference for students or researchers comparing humor theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor functions as a mechanism for releasing pent-up emotions or tension; laughter reduces psychological stress and discharges excess nervous or psychic energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains laughter as homeostatic release (tickling, anticipatory arousal reduced by mirth). Historical proponents include Spencer and Freud; used as a dramatic tool (Samuel Johnson). Researchers (e.g., Shurcliff, Lucas) frame humor as alternating strain/rest. Distinguishes tendentious (victimizing) and non-tendentious (victimless) humor; innocent 'jokework' disguises hostility making it socially acceptable. Empirical findings (Zillmann & Bryant) support combined effects of tendentious and innocuous elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor/laughter arises from a feeling of superiority over others — we laugh at misfortunes or defects because they make us feel superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical roots in Plato, Aristotle and Hobbes. Hobbes characterizes laughter as sudden 'glory' when recognizing one's superiority; typical evokers include: success beyond expectation, perceiving defects in others, perceiving past defects in oneself, and abstracted absurdities. Aristotle notes combination of incongruity and hostility. Kant allows harmless teasing in playful settings. Critics argue many types of humor lack superiority or that superiority feelings are distinct from the humor itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticisms of superiority theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenges to the adequacy of superiority as a general account of humor: many humorous phenomena do not involve superiority, and feelings of superiority are often distinct from the humorous response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical objections dating back to Beattie; modern scholars (Morreall, Levinson, Marra) maintain superiority cannot account for all humor and that affective reactions (e.g., superiority) may accompany but not constitute humor itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective disposition theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience moral judgments and dispositions toward characters affect amusement: people find it funnier when good things happen to liked people and bad things happen to disliked people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies how disposition toward victim and victor modulates mirth: more negative disposition toward disparaged agent increases mirth; more positive disposition toward victor increases mirth. Explains media/entertainment responses and why audiences enjoy seeing disliked characters harmed; also identifies limits when tragedy overwhelms laughter (evokes pity). Links to ethics of 'punching up' vs 'punching down' in comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity theory (incongruity-resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor depends on the perception of incongruity — a clash with expectation — often resolved by a cognitive shift or reinterpretation (surprise, sudden perspective change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers many forms (wordplay, riddle jokes, sudden twist). Historical proponents: Hutcheson, Kant (surprise/absurdity), Schopenhauer (recognition of incongruity), Bergson (mechanical versus living). Emphasizes resolution of cognitive dissonance (punchline causes reinterpretation). Variants discuss simultaneous contrast vs mental shift. Examples: riddles ('black and white and read all over').

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign Violation Theory (BVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor occurs when a situation simultaneously constitutes a violation (threatening one's sense of how the world ought to be) and is perceived as benign, with the observer able to hold both interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three conditions: (1) something threatens a normative expectation, (2) the threat seems benign, (3) the person perceives both interpretations at once. Explains tickling/play fighting, linguistic and moral norm violations, and why context/psychological distance/commitment to a norm modulate amusement. Empirical tests show e.g., church raffle vignette: commitment to sacred norms reduces benign interpretation and amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script-based Semantic Theory of Humor (SSTH)
rubrics_metrics.description: A linguistic theory for verbal jokes: a text must be compatible with two opposite semantic scripts and the punchline triggers an abrupt switch from the primary to the secondary script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two formal conditions: (i) text compatible with two different scripts, (ii) the two scripts are opposite (e.g., actual/non-actual, normal/abnormal, possible/impossible, good/bad, life/death, obscene/non-obscene). Example: 'Is the doctor at home?' joke — overlapping DOCTOR and LOVER scripts. Emphasizes script opposition and cultural dependence of scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Theory of Verbal Humor (GTVH) / Knowledge Resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Extends SSTH into six independent Knowledge Resources (KRs) for modeling and comparing verbal jokes: Script Opposition (SO), Logical Mechanism (LM), Situation (SI), Target (TA), Narrative Strategy (NS), and Language (LA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each KR: SO = script opposition; LM = mechanism connecting scripts (pun, faulty logic); SI = objects/props; TA = butt/target of joke (optional); NS = narrative format (dialogue, riddle, narrative); LA = wording/placement. KRs are hierarchically ordered (upper KRs constrain lower ones) and can be used to analyze joke similarity and variation (e.g., lightbulb joke variants). Allows categorization beyond single-line jokes to longer humorous texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer model of humor (Suslov)
rubrics_metrics.description: Models humor as an information-processing malfunction: a false version is quickly deleted from consciousness (incongruity-resolution) with timing playing a key role; explains verbal, visual, and tickling-based humor and individual differences biologically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adds timing to ambiguity role; deletion corresponds to neural network zeroing and release of excess neural energy producing motor reactions (laughter). Treats linguistic and visual humor equally; explains susceptibility differences, intonation role, nervous laughter, and why trite jokes fail. Suggests algorithmic realization requires extensive databases; supports evolutionary origins and comparisons with nonhuman play laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misattribution theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences misattribute why they laugh — they may believe they laugh at innocuous elements while underlying tendentious (hostile/taboo) elements drive the reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalized by Zillmann & Bryant (1980) and rooted in Freud: tendentious components (taboo, hostility) evoke laughter while observers misattribute amusement to innocent features. Explains why people laugh at victimization when hostilities are disguised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontic-epistemic theory of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter results from perceiving a cognitive impasse where social (normative) reality appears no longer factual — social reality conflicts with factual reality (Deculturation) or internal social contradictions (Relativisation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy produces a momentary collapse of social perception; laughter anesthetizes and resets social perception faculty, enabling forgetting of the comic stimulus and communicating the reaction socially. Related to Bergson's ideas about social reality vs factual reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual selection hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor evolved via sexual selection as a fitness signal (indicator) of desirable traits such as intelligence rather than direct survival advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed by Geoffrey Miller: humor indicates intelligence and other traits relevant to mate choice; explains why humor may have evolved despite limited direct survival value for early humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of mistaken reasoning theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor evolved to strengthen the brain's ability to find mistakes in active belief structures; the humorous mechanism aids detection of mistaken reasoning and practical problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hurley, Dennett, and Adams (2011) argue humor is adaptive for enhancing neural circuits for error detection. Connects to sexual selection as humor signals cognitive competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as defense mechanism (Vaillant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is an adaptive psychological defense (Vaillant's level 4): overtly expressing unpleasant or terrible ideas in a way that gives pleasure to self and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiates humor from wit (wit skirts distressing thoughts); humor enables confronting distressing material with pleasure. Useful concept in clinical/psychological accounts of coping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of humor versus sense of seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to distinguish when something is intended humorously or seriously is crucial; misuse can lead to 'bad taste' where humor crosses into unintended serious interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important when humor is used to make serious points (court jesters example) or when it unintentionally offends. Social/contextual awareness required to avoid crossing lines where the audience takes jokes literally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor, metonymy, and allegory in humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Figurative devices like metaphor, metonymy, and allegory play formal roles in creating humor via conceptual blending, structure-mapping, and poetic metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tony Veale, Koestler, Dedre Gentner, Lakoff & Johnson, and Fauconnier & Turner provide formal frameworks (structure-mapping, conceptual metaphor/blending) showing how metaphorical mapping generates humorous effects. Bakhtin emphasizes 'poetic metaphor' and allegory in humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: O'Shannon model of the comedic event
rubrics_metrics.description: A unified framework dividing comedic events into four interacting sections: context, information, aspects of awareness, and enhancers/inhibitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: reception factors prior to encounter; Information: cognitive processing and degree of incongruity; Aspects of awareness: internal reality, external role, effects on context/receivers; Enhancers/inhibitors: feelings like superiority, relief, aggression, identification, shock that modulate response. Model explains why jokes may rely on various mechanisms (e.g., low incongruity but strong superiority) and accounts for different responses (visceral vs appreciative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnoticed fall-back to former behavior patterns model
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter signals recognition of an unnoticed return to a former behavior pattern, unifying aspects of superiority and incongruity accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines laughter as acoustic signal to alert others to unnoticed fall-back; connects to ticklishness and evolutionary accounts (relation to bipedalism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bergson's theory (mechanism applied to life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic situations arise when mechanical rigidity/inflexibility is applied to living, elastic life; laughter has a social/moral role in correcting vices and enforcing uniformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include falls, imitations, absent-mindedness, repetitive gestures. Bergson frames laughter as an intellectual, emotionally detached activity; comic stems from apparent rigidity, not ugliness. Social role: collective activity that enforces norms by condemning ludicrous behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex systems / dynamic systems approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply complexity theory to humor: interacting parts of a system give rise to collective humorous behaviour; change and dynamics are central to understanding how jokes and running gags emerge and evolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for transdisciplinary research; applied to conversational humor, visual/verbal incongruity-resolution studies, and modeling joke birth and decline in discourse communities. Useful for studying emergence, spread, and dynamics of humor (e.g., memes, conversational jokes).
